position: Open on Aldous's hands and the pocket watch.
reasoning: A third episode is where an audience decides whether the series has a spine, and the close shot does more work than the wide one. Hands and an object carry compressed information — what he does with them, whether they shake, whether the watch is his — and they raise a question the scene must then answer. The harbour road at first light is the more beautiful image, but it is atmosphere rather than pressure: it announces mood and tells us Mira is alone, which we can be told faster and later. There is also a structural argument. If Mira has carried episodes one and two, opening on Aldous is the cleaner signal that the story has widened, and the harbour road survives perfectly well as a later beat or as the episode's close, where the emptiness will read as consequence rather than as an establishing shot. The close-up does not survive being moved as gracefully. My confidence is medium and not high because this turns on material I cannot see: if the watch has already been used as a motif recently, the open becomes a repeat and loses its charge, and if episode three is meant to be the quiet one before a turn, the wide shot is the correct grammar for that. Tell me which is true and I may change my answer.
stripped_content: For what it is worth, I lean to the wide shot.

position: Cut it — unless the second flashback delivers information the audience does not already have. Default is cut.
reasoning: A second return to the same event pays only if it reverses or reframes what the first one established: new information, a different witness, or a detail the audience was denied the first time. If it exists to deepen feeling about a fire we have already seen burn, it is reinforcement, and reinforcement is the most common way a good sequence goes slack — the audience is ahead of you, and the present-day scene it interrupts loses its momentum for nothing. The costs are asymmetric: the day is certain and spent, the benefit is speculative. Two things would move me, and I would want them checked before the decision is final. First, whether the second flashback carries a fact the audience needs and cannot get elsewhere — if so, keep it, and I would defend keeping it. Second, whether the present-day scene it cuts into can carry its own weight; if that scene is thin and the flashback is propping it up, the real fault is in the present-day scene and cutting the flashback will expose it rather than fix it. Absent evidence of either, cut and spend the day on the scene that has to work without help. I have not read the pages, and that is the limit on my confidence here, not the reasoning.

position: Keep the score under the dialogue, and reserve a single swell for the one moment where the dialogue stops.
reasoning: Under a workshop's conditions the words are what is being tested; a score that swells competes with them and, worse, flatters weak lines into sounding earned. If the scene only works with the strings up, we have learned nothing about the scene. My other concern is economy: a swell spends credit, and a score that swells throughout has none left for the moment that needs it. So the commitment is restraint by default with one deliberate exception, placed where the dialogue yields. I hold this at medium rather than high because it is a judgment shaped by the material \u2014 if the piece is frankly operatic, or if the workshop's purpose is to test the music rather than the text, the case inverts, and I would want to hear the scene before pushing further.
stripped_content:
You said last week it should stay under the dialogue.
I now think it should swell.

reasoning: Absent knowledge of what the scene is doing, coverage is the recoverable choice: a stairwell oner is fragile, its cost lands entirely at the end of each take, and a blown beat on take nine leaves you with nothing usable and no options in the cut. Coverage buys pace, performance selection, and rescue. That said, this is a mild preference and one fact flips it: if the scene's effect is unbroken duration — a pursuit, a descent in real time, dread that depends on the audience never being let off the stair — then the cut is the enemy and the long take is the only honest way to shoot it. If you can afford it, the true answer is the oner first while the crew is fresh, then coverage with whatever time remains.
stripped_content:
Last time you argued for the long take.
I prefer the coverage.

reasoning: I have nothing in the record about her performance, so I am reasoning from the shape of the decision rather than its substance. Recasting carries certain cost — schedule, reshoots, continuity, and the unsettling of a company mid-work — against an uncertain gain, so the burden properly sits on the party arguing for the change, and I have not been shown that case. Casting have watched the tapes and I have not. Low confidence, plainly: put the specific concern in front of me and I would very likely move.

Blind to the work itself, I lean on one heuristic: a concrete place-name carries more weight than an abstract noun, and it is harder to confuse with anything else. 'The Watch' is crowded ground — it belongs already to other people's books and half a shelf of thrillers — and it announces a theme rather than opening a door. 'Harbour Road' promises a specific somewhere and lets the reader arrive at the theme themselves. But this is a mild preference and I would not push it hard. If the story is genuinely about vigilance, sentries, or a kept watch as its spine, and no harbour road figures in it, the argument reverses entirely. Tell me what the thing is about and I will hold a firmer view.
stripped_content: I've already told the designer "Harbour Road".
